A build-along course

Building Tessera

A collaborative canvas. Two people draw on the same board at the same moment and both edits survive. One of them goes through a tunnel, keeps working, and everything they did arrives intact when the signal comes back. No server decides who wins, because no server is asked. Built from an empty folder, with every bug found along the way written down.

24 chapters SvelteKit 3Svelte 5 runesCRDTs from scratchLocal-first
Start chapter 01 →

Everything we'll cover

  1. 01 What we are building Tessera: a collaborative canvas for system diagrams that keeps working with the network off, and merges everything back without asking anybody to choose.
  2. 02 Who decides who wins Three designs for two people editing one thing, why the first two are the ones everybody builds, and what a conflict-free type actually promises.
  3. 03 Setting up: a SvelteKit 3 project Node, pnpm, the folder, and the single biggest change in SvelteKit 3 — there is no svelte.config.js any more.
  4. 04 Environment variables that cannot be wrong `src/env.ts` and `defineEnvVars` — declaring every variable once, validating at boot, and making a secret in the browser something you have to type on purpose.
  5. 05 The map of the project Every folder, what lives in it, and the rule that decides which folder a new file goes in.
  6. 06 Time that cannot go backwards Why `Date.now()` cannot decide who wins, what a hybrid logical clock is, and the drift guard that was in the wrong tier for a fortnight.
  7. 07 What have I already seen? A four-line version vector, made possible by the last chapter — and the afternoon lost to using it for the wrong job.
  8. 08 Room between any two things Stacking order without renumbering: base-62 keys that always have a gap, and the tiebreak that stops two replicas rendering the same data differently.
  9. 09 Which shapes exist The resurrection bug, why a tombstone is not the fix, and why "add wins" is the forgiving direction.
  10. 10 The fields on a shape Twenty-two lines of actual code, one rule of thumb for when to use them, and the `undefined` return that turns out to matter.
  11. 11 Two people typing in one label RGA — an identity per character, a tree rather than the famous scan, and the counterexample that shows why.
  12. 12 Proving it, as far as it can be proved A property test that builds a few hundred thousand hostile delivery schedules — and the two real bugs it found within a dozen seeds.
  13. 13 Eight operations, and nothing else The vocabulary of a board, the operation algebra every change goes through, and why validation matters more in a CRDT than anywhere else.
  14. 14 The model and the projection Two representations of one board, why they are not collapsed into one, and the listener bug that made undo work perfectly while nothing reached the network.
  15. 15 Keeping the projection honest Model to view: writing the smallest possible amount into `$state`, and the ordering detail that stops a half-built node reaching a component.
  16. 16 Snapshots, and what may never be forgotten Writing a document out deterministically, the clock bug that only appeared after a refresh, and the tombstones that can never be collected.
  17. 17 A database that stores operations Tenancy, boards, and an append-only log whose primary key is the server’s total order — plus the unique index that makes a retry free.
  18. 18 Four roles, checked per operation Why a single check at connection time is a suggestion rather than a permission system, and the 404 that stops a board id being an oracle.
  19. 19 The only way in Four gates in order, one transaction, and the broadcast slice that assumed duplicates arrive as a prefix.
  20. 20 Telling everybody else An in-memory hub that is explicitly not a delivery guarantee, and a server-sent event stream that subscribes before it reads.
  21. 21 A tab’s identity, and what crosses the network One actor per tab and why that is a requirement rather than a simplification — plus two channels with opposite guarantees.
  22. 22 The outbox Sixty lines of IndexedDB wrapper, one compound key, and the `oncomplete` that is the difference between "saved" being true and being a message.
  23. 23 The sync engine Three steps in order, four honest states, a stream with real backoff, and a flush with a lock.
  24. 24 Four bugs in one file A stranded flush, a bad slice, a watermark from the wrong place, and an echo filter — all the same mistake, seen four times.

Every chapter shows the real code from the finished project in tessera. Type it out rather than pasting where you can — the errors you make and fix are the part that sticks. A dozen chapters end with a bug that was genuinely in this codebase, what it looked like from the outside, and how it was cornered.
